text: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers Automatic differentiation (AD) evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the elementary operations in a program. It supplies Jacobians for Newton iterations, directional derivatives for Krylov methods, and sensitivities for parameter estimation. These are shared numerical foundations across many physical models. Implemented here: a small forward-mode dual-number engine and a comparison of analytic differentiation, finite differences and AD on the existing Bratu boundary-value problem. The experiment reuses the atlas's Armijo-damped Newton solver. Reverse mode, implicit sensitivities and adjoints are explained as connections; this exhibit does not implement them. Four ways to obtain a derivative An analytic derivative is derived mathematically and entered into the solver by hand. It can expose structure and provide an independent reference, but the derivative must be kept consistent with the residual implementation. Symbolic differentiation manipulates expressions into another expression. AD instead carries numerical derivative information through the evaluated operations, without constructing a global symbolic formula. Finite differences estimate a derivative from perturbed function values. For a vector residual F and a direction v, forward and centered differences are Dε+F(u)v=F(u+εv)−F(u)ε,Dε0F(u)v=F(u+εv)−F(u−εv)2ε.Dε+​F(u)v=εF(u+εv)−F(u)​,Dε0​F(u)v=2εF(u+εv)−F(u−εv)​. For sufficiently smooth F, their truncation errors are first and second order in ε. A very small ε amplifies cancellation and rounding in the residual evaluations. The useful step depends on the state, direction, precision and scaling of F. A finite-difference check should therefore sweep several steps. AD has no finite-difference step or associated truncation error. It still uses floating-point arithmetic: unstable formulas, overflow, underflow and rounding can affect both values and derivatives. The differentiated object is the composition of real-arithmetic operations represented by the executed program, evaluated numerically. It is not the derivative of the discontinuous mapping from one set of floating-point bit patterns to another. Forward mode: carry a value and a direction Seed the input with a direction v and propagate pairs consisting of a value and its directional derivative. Dual-number notation makes the chain rule visible: a^=a+ηa˙,η2=0,a^b^=ab+η(a˙b+ab˙),exp⁡(a^)=exp⁡(a)+ηexp⁡(a)a˙.a=a+ηa˙,η2=0,ab=ab+η(a˙b+ab˙),exp(a)=exp(a)+ηexp(a)a˙. The nilpotent symbol η is an algebraic device, not a small numerical step. The implementation stores the two arrays separately. It overloads the small set of operations needed for this experiment, including elementwise arithmetic, indexing, exponentiation and multiplication by a constant matrix. Unsupported operations are outside this educational engine's scope. For F from n inputs to m outputs, one seeded execution returns F(u) and J(u)v. This Jacobian–vector product (JVP) avoids storing an m-by-n Jacobian. Seed each coordinate basis vector in turn to assemble all n columns. The Bratu comparison deliberately uses that transparent assembly; it does not exploit sparsity coloring or provide a matrix-free Newton solver. Reverse mode and the derivative you actually need Reverse mode propagates an output weight w backwards through local derivative rules to obtain J(u)ᵀw, often called a vector–Jacobian product (VJP). For a scalar objective with many parameters, one reverse pass can produce its gradient. An implementation commonly retains intermediate values or recomputes them through checkpointing. Forward mode is attractive when only a few input directions are required. The relevant dimensions are the numbers of independent inputs and outputs, together with the requested products. A Hessian–vector product for a smooth scalar objective can be obtained by differentiating its gradient in a direction. Explicitly assembling a Hessian is unnecessary when an optimization method only needs that product. See Baydin et al. (2018) for an AD survey and the JAX autodiff cookbook for practical JVP, VJP and higher-order constructions. JAX is a reading reference; the local experiment requires only the atlas's existing NumPy environment. The analytic Jacobian is an independent formula. Finite differences and AD both evaluate the same residual function. In particular, AD differentiates the discrete residual F; it does not remove the centered stencil's spatial discretization error. The exact continuous solution is used to check spatial refinement, not as an exact root of the discrete equations. Verification: hold the problem fixed The saved measurements and source hashes separate three checks so that accurate derivatives and accurate PDE solutions are not confused. The derivative check uses n=31 and the state u_*(x_i)+0.05 sin(3πx_i), away from the exact continuous profile. Its direction is sin(2πx_i)+0.3 cos(5πx_i), normalized to unit Euclidean length. The sweep contains 29 logarithmically spaced, absolute perturbations from 1 down to 10⁻¹⁴; these are derivative perturbations, not spatial mesh widths. Differentiate at a fixed state. Compare the assembled forward-mode AD Jacobian and its JVP against the analytic formula. Sweep finite-difference steps at that same state, using both forward and centered differences. Report relative Frobenius errors for matrices and relative Euclidean errors for directional products. A deterministic smooth direction prevents run-to-run changes in the comparison. Solve the same discrete system. Start every Newton solve at zero, use the same residual, Armijo search, dense linear solve and residual tolerance, and change only how the Jacobian is supplied. The finite-difference run uses a fixed centered-difference step recorded in the manifest. Measure the true residual after each accepted iteration and compare the final roots with the analytic-Jacobian solve. Refine the mesh. Repeat the three methods for n=15, 31 and 63 interior nodes. Compare their roots with u_* at the interior nodes using a nodal maximum error. Approximately fourfold error reduction under halving h identifies the centered scheme's second-order spatial behavior. In the saved run, AD and the analytic Jacobian agree entry by entry, while the relative JVP error is about 8×10⁻¹⁶. This exact matrix agreement is specific to the operation ordering in this example, not a general guarantee of bitwise agreement for AD. The finite-difference curves show the useful range between truncation error and cancellation. All nine Newton solves reach the common absolute residual Euclidean tolerance 10⁻¹⁰ in three updates. The fixed centered-difference perturbation is 10⁻⁵; its final roots agree with the analytic-Jacobian roots to less than 10⁻¹⁴ in nodal maximum norm. The continuous nodal maximum errors are approximately 1.738×10⁻⁴, 4.337×10⁻⁵ and 1.084×10⁻⁵ on the three grids. Their factor-of-four reduction remains after changing the derivative calculation: spatial discretization sets the leading solution error here. The matrix norm includes entries of size h⁻². A small relative matrix error can therefore hide errors in smaller terms. The direct directional check is reported separately, rather than relying only on a product of the assembled finite-difference matrix. The analytic derivative is a reference, not an assumption that every analytic implementation is correct. The tests also check derivative rules on separate functions and nontrivial directions, and check Bratu refinement against the continuous solution. Agreement between two Jacobians alone would not validate the boundary conditions or the PDE discretization. The figure makes no speed ranking. Assembling a dense AD Jacobian here needs n forward seeds; centered differences need two residual evaluations per column. Counts describe these implementations, not equal-cost operations or the best sparse AD strategy. For a large Newton–Krylov method, supplying Jv directly can be preferable to constructing every column, while a suitable preconditioner remains necessary. Connections to implicit integration and parameter estimation An implicit ODE stage has a residual involving the state and time step. Its Newton matrix contains derivatives of the ODE right-hand side, so the same AD construction can supply them. For parameter estimation, derivatives of observations or an objective with respect to model parameters connect a simulation to an optimization method. Derivative availability does not itself choose a stable integrator, a well-conditioned parameterization or a convergent optimization algorithm. Suppose the converged discrete state satisfies F(u,θ)=0. At a differentiable solution with nonsingular F_u, its parameter sensitivity satisfies Fududθ=−Fθ.Fu​dθdu​=−Fθ​. Differentiating a fixed, finite sequence of Newton iterations instead gives the derivative of that sequence, including its dependence on the initial guess. Stopping criteria and line-search branches complicate that distinction. Near a singular Jacobian, sensitivities can be large even when the primal residual is small. Primal and derivative solve tolerances therefore need separate checks. These sensitivity and adjoint equations are explanatory extensions; the present Bratu exhibit compares Jacobians used in the primal solve. Limits: smoothness, branches and numerical stability AD applies the derivative rules of the operations that are executed. At a branch boundary, an absolute-value corner or a limiter switch, the underlying function may have no unique classical derivative; a library's chosen rule does not establish one. Adaptive time-step decisions can change the executed path under parameter perturbations. For shocks, a computed grid-value derivative also needs interpretation in terms of shock motion and the quantity being measured. The discretized derivative should be checked for mesh and time-step convergence when it is intended to approximate a continuous sensitivity. Differentiating a discretized solver and discretizing continuous sensitivity or adjoint equations require their own consistency analysis. Stable function evaluation matters too: a formula that overflows in the primal calculation is not repaired by applying the chain rule.
